title: Akshata Murty on Keeping Bengaluru Diwali Traditions Alive in Britain
excerpt: At the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan's Diwali fundraiser in London, Akshata Murty recalled lighting diyas and cooking rasam at Downing Street and credited the Bhavan with preserving her family's cultural roots.
body:
• Akshata Murty, businesswoman and spouse of former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, spoke at the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan's annual Diwali fundraiser in London about keeping her family's cultural traditions alive at Downing Street.
  • She recalled lighting diyas and cooking traditional dishes such as rasam in the official quarters while Sunak served as Chancellor and then as Prime Minister.
  • She credited the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan with a pivotal role in preserving her family's cultural roots, according to agency reporting of her address.
  • The Bhavan's own record lists Murty as Guest of Honour at its Diwali Gala on November 22, 2025 at the Nobu Hotel London, with her father, Infosys founder Narayana Murthy, as Special Guest — a concrete example of the Bengaluru-rooted family traditions she described being carried into British public life.

Akshata Murty, the businesswoman and spouse of Britain's first Indian-origin prime minister, Rishi Sunak, has opened up about the blend of cultural traditions in the couple's life at Downing Street. In an address at the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan's annual Diwali fundraiser in London, she spoke of the Bhavan's pivotal role in preserving her family's cultural roots, according to agency reporting carried by Devdiscourse.

Diwali inside Downing Street

During the fundraiser, Murty reminisced about celebrating Diwali at one of the world's most recognisable residences. She recounted lighting diyas and cooking traditional dishes, such as rasam, in the official quarters while Sunak served as Chancellor and as Prime Minister. The detail matters because it describes a private family practice carried into an official residence: the festival was not only hosted for guests, it was cooked and lit at home, in the quarters where the family lived.

The Bhavan's role

Murty's address centred on the institution hosting her. She spoke of the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan's pivotal role in preserving her family's cultural roots. The Bhavan's official London Kendra page records the shape of that relationship: at its Diwali Gala on November 22, 2025, held at the Nobu Hotel London, Portman Square, Akshata Murty Sunak, described as a businesswoman and philanthropist, was the Guest of Honour. Her father, Padma Vibhushan Sri Narayana Murthy CBE, founder of Infosys, was the Special Guest, and Vikram Doraiswami, the High Commissioner of India to the UK, was the Chief Guest.

The Bhavan's account of the evening describes a musical ensemble by its students, composed and conducted by resident sitar teacher Ustad Mehboob Nadeem, followed by speeches and classical dance performances: Kathak by students of Abhinav Shankar Mishra and Shreetama Mukherjee, Bharatanatyam by students of Guru Prakash Yadagudde, and a closing ensemble of Odissi, Kathak and Kuchipudi. Agency reporting of the fundraiser also noted support from Narayana Murthy and said the centre's challenges, including local parking restrictions, were addressed by Chairman Subhanu Saxena and High Commissioner Vikram Doraiswami, who emphasised the Bhavan's integral role in UK-India cultural relations.

Why it resonates for the diaspora

Murty was brought up in Bengaluru, and the traditions she described — diyas lit at home and a South Indian dish cooked in the kitchen — are the household version of Diwali that many diaspora families recognise. Her account places that household practice inside Britain's most famous official home during the years when her husband led the government, first as Chancellor and then as prime minister. For readers in Britain and elsewhere in the diaspora, the practical thread in her remarks is institutional as much as personal: a cultural centre such as the Bhavan in London is presented as the place that helps a family keep those roots across generations, through classes, performances and an annual Diwali gathering that brings students, patrons and artists together.

The Bhavan's London programme continues through the year with music, dance and literary events listed on its official page. Readers who want to attend a future Diwali Gala or a class can check the Kendra's listings there for dates and venues.
